This audio is a fragment edited for "Merganetta - A Short Film", a documentary by colombian audiovisual artist León Felipe Jiménez. It has been panned and I used a moderate high pass filter and an agressive low pass filter, nevertheless I was careful to use these filters only til the point they wouldn't change the tone of the duck's sound. 

This quacking corresponds to a male duck leading the female and 1 offspring river upwards, the male went first to explore as they perceived the presence of another duck (a toy of a duck we used to call their attention). The male would make this noise as he approached the intruder fake duck. Though the male seemed to be concerned about the intruder's presence, he wasn't scared.

rmk: Very long sequence of one adult male singing on forest edge , it was not clear for me the context of the song but I presumed could be territorial because I heard another male (previous recordings) doing similar vocalizations in front of one female. I want to dedicate this recording to the memory of the colombian biologist Gustavo Kattan who unfortunately passed away some weks ago. He was a very influential conservation biologist and ornithologist in Colombia and the neotropics as well, and made long term studies with birds mainly in the central andes in Otum Quimbaya sanctuary and western andes near Cali. One of his favorite and most studies  groups were precisely the cracids, particularly the Cauca guan.This my personal way to make a tribute to his legacy in research, conservation and education. Andres Angulo.

rmk: Distant bird singing in the forest. The bird was already singing when we turned off the generator at 21:00, with singing continuing for another 15 minutes or so. Another briefer song bout took place around 22:00. The night was quite overcast, and no Nocturnal Curassows were heard during two previous nights of camping here earlier in the week when the nights were clear. The bird was singing again the next night, which was also overcast.

Feeding secretively along a well-vegetated river, in the wet mud close to the river edge. Calling at less than 15m away, and eventually appeared in full view about 6m from me. Yellow-knobbed Curassow were seen feeding on the other side of the river about 20m away.

The recording hasn't been modified significantly, just some gain and equalization adjustments to reduce the rain sound. It was raining softly and there was a lot of mist. The sound was coming from the ground approximately 10 meters from us.

* Bill snapping from a couple of individuals found foraging with a HUGE army ants swarm. The ants were of a smaller kind and most likely Labidus sp. The swarm was attended by: White-plumed Antbird · Pithys albifrons, White-cheeked Antbird · Gymnopithys leucaspis, Common Scale-backed Antbird · Willisornis poecilinotus, Black-throated Antbird · Myrmeciza atrothorax, Coraya Wren · Pheugopedius coraya, Plain-brown Woodcreeper · Dendrocincla fuliginosa, and White-crowned Manakin · Dixiphia pipra.

* Habitat was white-sand forest actually with some flooded areas (not near várzea/igapó though) and not as stated in HBW: "to date found exclusively in well-drained terra firme forest with 20–25 m-high canopy".

* This is the first confirmed record of this species for Colombia and represents a range extension of more than 150 km N of its traditional distribution in Amazonian lowlands of Colombia.

* Observation made with my mate Jorge González and the superb local guide and friend Miguel Portura both from EtnoAvesVaupes, and clients Joe Church and Bill Mossey.

rmk: Cerca al Pantano de Martos, en un área de Páramo azonal encontré una pareja de Trogon personatus en vegetación de arbusto alto, adyacente en la via. En este caso noté que el macho presenta un anillo ocular rojo y su pico es completamente amarillo y la banda blanca en el pecho. Inicialmente asocio a este taxón como temperatus, debido a que es una raza que se encuentra en elevaciones de montaña (en este caso 2900 msnm) y por sus caracterisiticas fenotípicas, pero es solo una hipotesis mia, en tal caso, representa una buena vocalización de esta especie para esta región.

file-name: XC149226-001_A_010_Sergio_Trogon personatus hembra llamndo a volanton con alimento en pico_2012_12_30.mp3
rmk:
Adriana Sua escuchó inicialmente la vocalización de un ave, desconocida, buscó y se pudo dar cuenta que se trataba de los llamados de una hembra de T. persontus la cual tenía en el pico una larva verde. Pasados unos 15 minutos llegue con un amigo al sitio y Adriana nos comentó que este individuo no dejaba de realizar estos llamados sin consumir la larva y realizando movimientos de un lado para otro del camino (desplazamiento no más de 5 metros de un punto a otro).

Más al fondo pero con otro tipo de vocalización escuchamos otro Trogon el cual pudimos observar y se trataba de un macho que poseía en su pico un insecto (parecía una libélula), pero a diferencia de la hembra su vocalización era diferente (leve sonido de fondo) y no realizó movimientos, se quedó estático en una percha a unos 8 metros de la hembra. Al principio creíamos que se trataba de alguna especie de cortejo, pero nos dimos cuenta minutos después de que estábamos en lo incorrecto.

Después de varios minutos, un poco más de 15 adicionales a la primera observacion de Adriana, paso sobre nosotros volando (vuelo torpe) una “bola” café la cual se poso en cercanías a la hembra, cuando observamos con detenimiento vimos que se trataba de un volantón del Trogon. Y entonces allí comprendimos, que la hembra y el macho con sus llamados lo que estaban era intentando que el volantón se desplazara, volara y para esto que mejor forma de atraerlo que con alimento. El volantón permaneció en el mismo lugar por unos 10 a 15 minutos y la hembra mientras tanto seguía haciendo llamados y alejándose y acercándose al volantón sin dar el alimento. En ocasiones se acercaba a menos de 50 cm y se alejaba de nuevo a máximo 5 metros. Después de esto el volantón salió volando, la hembra detrás (el macho nunca apareció en escena después) seguido de un silencio en el bosque, la hembra dejo de hacer los llamados.

Foto Neil Díaz (hembra y volantón) http://www.flickr.com/photos/neilorlandodiazmartinez/8332735100/in/set-72157632402738658

Se descubrió localidad por congruencia geográfica entre los valles altos del cercano rio Pescado y el Bodoquero (lugar de esta grabación), y siguiendo la presencia de estratos sedimentarios cretácicos sobre estratos volcánicos del jurásico que usa esta especie para sus nidos.

La grabación se obtubo a partir de un video captado por una cámara Nikon COOLPIX P510. 

Este fue la última  vocalización de las cuatro que hizo el halcón.

Se observó en el dosel de un árbol de Eucalipto (Eucalyptus sp.), sobre una rama gruesa dispuesta de manera horizontal. Este árbol se encuentra próximo a otros eucaliptos, otros árboles nativos, y pastizales, en una matriz urbanizada con edificios con más de 10 pisos y algunas casas con amplias zonas verdes. Muy cerca de los eucaliptos hay un cuerpo de agua de origen artificial de unos 100m x 100m. 

En este lugar se ha podido también observar otras rapaces como el Águila pescadora (Pandion haliaetus), Gavilán aliancho (Buteo platypterus), y un Esmerejón (Falco columbarius).

The vocalization of interest is similar to Thripadectes virgaticeps, and indeed to my ear is virtually identical to XC245051.

However, I am not confident that XC245051 is correctly identified.  All other recordings of T. virgaticeps on XC show a strong fundamental near 3-4 kHz, and a strong overtone generally around 6-9 kHz (e.g. XC387707 ).

My mystery and XC245051 show a fundamental at 5-6 kHz and a weak overtone series as expected.

I freely admit that these cuts sound quite similar to more typical T. virgaticeps, but I would appreciate additional input on whether they are truly a variation of that species, or are something else entirely.

This recording was cut to remove loud dictated notes.  Considerable time was removed (including vocalizations of interested covered over by dictated notes) in both of the brief silences.  The vocalizations on the cut were delivered in a long dawn-song series with intervals typical of the intact second half of the cut (vocalizations near 0:06.5 and 0:12 ).

rmk:
A very elusive bird; its plumage was not highly contrastant with the vegetation and it moved very rapidly from branch to branch. It sang very frequently from several perching points in the scrub vegetation, at ∼3-6 m in height. The scrub was on the border of a road in the countryside, and separate it from pastures. The area was formerly covered by bmh-MB. During my observations, it apparently was only resting and cleaning itself, alternating those activities with moderately long vocalization sessions. Some other species in the immediate surrounding environment were Tiaris olivaceus, Sporophila nigricollis, Zenaida auriculata, Columbina tapacolti and cf. Troglodytes aedon. I used a playback to provoque an answer call, but it didn't answer in response and limited only to look around to try to find the origin of the sound. 

Note: The recording was edited in Ocean Audio. I normalized it to -3 db and changed the recording format (mp3) into .WAV.

file-name: XC166806-Yapacana Antbird female calls after playback Inirida 060214.MP3
rmk: Calls (alarm calls?) from female responding to playback of male song (XC64219). After about two minutes of playback, this female responded strongly by approaching to within 5-10 meters and calling almost continuously for 2-3 minutes. The bird kept quite low in the dense understory (generally within 50 cm of the ground) and moved rather erratically, often flicking/wagging its tail. Further playback after about five minutes elicited a diminished response (the bird resumed calling but did not approach, while a second bird of unknown sex was also heard calling in the distance), and after a few more minutes the bird(s) eventually lost interest. No males were heard singing or seen.
Same bird as XC284843.

rmk: Visit to Puerto Inírida with Pablo Florez, Guilherme Brito and John Lobel to study this Thamnophilus, discovered at Inírida by PF in August 2016, and here provisionally assigned to T. palliatus, in recognition of its apparently closer morphological similarity to the latter, rather than to T. tenuepunctatus. This is one of a series of recordings of a male, different to that in XC499361, which inhabited a recently cleared chacra, still with a good number of Cecropia and bushy growth at its edges. For more information about these birds see: Florez, P. (2017) A mysterious antshrike in eastern Colombia. Neotrop. Birding 20: 21-24.

rmk: First record of Cocha Antshrike for Colombia, discovered by myself and Jurgen Beckers. Alarm (?) calls of a male and female responding aggressively to playback in dense understory (about 1.5 -2 m off the ground) of streamside forest (the forest is presumably flooded at this spot for most of the year; water levels were very low). These calls were uttered immediately after the birds - which had been silent - flew in aggressively in response to playback of Cocha Antshrike song. After about two minutes of making these calls, the birds began to sing quite persistently (XC302791), which they continued to do for at least 15 minutes. Photographic documentation on eBird checklists.

I heard one (male?) in forest interior from the ground. Microhabitat is defined by a high concentration of epiphytes, especially bromeliads, orchids and arboreal ferns and dark shade (more 90% of tree crown cover). Understory is very closed and canopy has a low height. Interestingly this forest is relatively young (30 years). People from the Village told me, that the place was completely cutted 50 years ago. But after a familiar conflict between owners, they decided to left the location untouched( without agriculture and cattle). After this, the forest regenerated in almost 20 years. I also registered other forest specialists in this patch. This and other observations suggest me that the andean avifauna in this part of Antioquia, included forest specialists, can recolonize forest habitats retatively fast. If their habitat does not suffer structural degradation after natural regrowth. Off course we need quantitative data for testing this.  Recording distance was 20 meters.

Recording archived at **IAvH-BSA 19217** (Colección de Sonidos-Instituto Humboldt). One or maybe two individuals in this recording, which includes a natural song bout and two calls (at 7.5 and 26.5 sec). This was made in a ridge in the middle of a continuous cloud forest at 1550 m. Bodega Vieja is the type locality of this "Antioquia *Myiopagis*" and one of several cloud forest sites in the Amalfi-Anorí region of the northern Central cordillera where we've discovered this rare bird, which was provisionally reported as *M. caniceps* (rightly so!) in [Ornitología Neotropical {2008}19:495–515](http://www.museum.lsu.edu/cuervo/pubs_files/Cuervo_etalON2008.pdf). In Amalfi, adults "*M. olallai*" look like [this](https://www.flickr.com/photos/amcuervo/15323404029) - and quite similar to specimens from the Serranía de Perijá. Check out our forthcoming paper in Zootaxa

Recording archived at **IAvH-BSA 19187** (Colección de Sonidos-Instituto Humboldt). A bird in the canopy of a heavily disturbed small fragment (19 Ha.). This was in an Andean, mid-elevation cloud forest at 1550 m at the northern end of the Central cordillera. A short segment of its voice was used for playback but elicited very little or no response. Co-workers and I have documented this bird (as "*M. caniceps*") in the Amalfi-Anorí region between 1300-1850 m (see [Ornitología Neotropical {2008}19:495–515](http://www.museum.lsu.edu/cuervo/pubs_files/Cuervo_etalON2008.pdf)). And this is how this ["Antioquia *Myiopagis*"](https://www.flickr.com/photos/amcuervo/15503418052/) look. The question is, how do they sound in Serranía de Perijá?

Recording archived at **IAvH-BSA 19580** (Colección de Sonidos-Instituto Humboldt). Two song bouts of the same individual. These recordings were made in a large fragment of pluvial premontane forest. Bosque Guayabito is one of several cloud forest sites in the Amalfi-Anorí region of the northern Central cordillera where we've discovered this "Antioquia Myiopagis", which was provisionally reported as *M. caniceps* (rightly so!) in [Ornitología Neotropical {2008}19:495–515](http://www.museum.lsu.edu/cuervo/pubs_files/Cuervo_etalON2008.pdf). A specimen (eventually the paratype) was taken at this locality on 4 January 2005: does it look to you like a [*M. olallai*](https://www.flickr.com/photos/amcuervo/15323404029)? The holotype is from a different locality, also in Amalfi. Check out our forthcoming paper in Zootaxa

This bird was seen and heard. I recorded its vocalization, but I didn't take visual records by camera. During my observations, it repeatedly flew between several trees, even crossing a considerably extense open area. Specifically, during the recording, it was perching on a little branch of Psidium sp. I saw it both while being on middle levels of the canopy and on the floor. Apparently, it fed on both levels, but only stayed resting on little branches, never on the floor. It showed the typical tyranids' movement of jumping-flying on/over the same point. It vocalized very frequently while foraging, and moved very rapidly through the foliage. Area was basically covered by bamboo colonies and secondary forests in early sucession. Finally, audio belongs to an only one individual, during only one vocalization session.

Posted initially as a mystery, but quickly resolved by Jorge Alcalá, after which I added the species. I hope that's the correct approach here.

Noted as "elaenia sp." but possibly some other type of new world flycatcher. Smaller than Yellow-bellied Elaenia, probably general size of Empidonax. Recording seems plausible for Lesser Elaenia but very clearly has two syllables and sounds to have none of the burry, raspy quality of most elaenia and most recordings I have listened to of Lesser Elaenia. Sounds quite like some two-syllable recordings of Yellow-bellied Flycatcher, which should not occur here. Bird was in a solitary tree in a clearing inside a very open and comparatively well-vegetated condominium development, the Marina de Barú, nominally dry coastal forest, here cleared and landscaped.

rmk: ID accurancy: 90%.  Habitat: Secondary forest. Code: OHM020A_0118  Empidonax virescens.  Equipment: Marantz PMD 222 with Sennheiser ME 66, TDK 60 SA-II.

The recording has not been modified at all. The bird was located in a strip of riparian vegetation dominated by Guadua angustifolia (native bamboo species) on the edge of a cattle farm (with moderate tree cover and other crops e.g., citrus, shade-coffee). The bird generally moved between 2 and 5 m from the ground, though the terrain is quite steeply sloped. It behaved as a fairly typical Empidonax flycatcher - sitting still for long periods of time, pumping its tail regularly, flycatching and returning to the same spot, or to a new spot. It changed perches frequently (every ~30 seconds). Weather was overcast, little to no wind.

Field Marks: weak crest, very faint whitish eyering (with very faint trace of a teardrop effect), orange lower mandible with dusky tip, bill length approximately equal to the distance between start of bill and back of eye, drab olive back and nape, two yellowish wingbars (upper bar appeared brownish at times), yellow margins on secondaries, moderate to long primary projection (I'm bad at judging that fieldmark), grayish-white throat, drab olive (dusky) breast, pale yellow belly and vent, medium length tail (shorter than folded wing length).

Field marks taken from photos, can send if desired.

loc: Tayrona National Park, Santa Marta, Magdalena. In the trail between el Cabo San Juan and Arrecifes.
rmk: A lek of this species was detected at forest interior in the trail between Cabo San Juan and arrecifes. Three  males were seen singing and jumping along the branches, several displays were noted. First two males (probably juveniles) were placed in a branch 3 meters hight and began to make alternated jumpings for at least the first two minutes. Then  other male probably older began to hop quickly along the branches moving faster its wings and vocalizing. This last one minute. During this time the other two juvenile males continuing jumping until one of them moves faster and flew outside to other exposed perch. This was at  4 minute. Finally the older male changed of perch and began to do short flies along the branch while the other males were jumping. This part was not coordinated between juvenile males. This ocurred during the final  minute. The jumpings of the males involved very short twists of less of 20 cm of height  over the branch. But the older male never was close to the other males in the lek. The female was not seen. The aproximate area of the lek was perhaps 30 m2? (based on the movements of the older male). Recording distance was aprox 5 meters between I and the 2 juveniles and 9 meters between I and the older male.

Habitat: Bosque secundario, bosque seco. 
Comportamiento: Dos machos bailando. Primero ambos machos estaban a una altura de aproximadamente 3 metros del suelo y cantaban lo que se oye hasta el minuto 1:04. Luego ambos se posaron sobre una percha a escasos centímetros del suelo (20 cm aprox.) y empezaron a hacer un sonido diferente (min 1:13 a 1:49). Mientras hacen este sonido, el macho " A" saltó sobre el macho "B". Inmediatamente B se movió a la misma ubicación en donde estuvo A  y luego A saltó sobre B y esta serie de moviemientos se repitió hasta el minuto 1:49.   El baile consistía en hacer círculos entre los dos. Pronto subiremos fotos que Felipe tomó y las publicaremos para facilitar la explicación.  En el minuto 1:49 cada individuo vocaliza un silbido muy intenso, hacen un salto de aprox. 50 cm de alto y se alejan volando rápidamente en direcciones opuestas. Su baile fue un hermoso espectáculo.

A male was  seen and heard at riparian vegetation adjacent to a small patch of premontane forest. Male was placed at a Philodendron leaf (Araceae) and was observed doing stylized displays which includes some hops and quick tail movements. female was seen only briefly and only did some short movements but she was not seen that were singing. I recorded 4 song types of the same male. This is the first cut that corresponds to the first song type, int his case is the tipical "call" of this species a guttural “chu-r-r-k”  (Kroodsma and Brewer 2005). Recording distance was 5 meters. I amplified the cut ( 4 db).  Before this call was  labeled in a previus recording with  XC327014 as the original number. I decided to delete this original recording for several reasons. First It did not have a good volume so its sonogram was of very limited value for many reasons (scientific research, education, etc). Second it was too long that the 4 song types delivered by the male were missing in the first recording and again in the sonogram. Third In the original cut it was not evident the realization of these 4 song types and the vocalization was though as a duet (but females was not seen singing, I erronusly assumed this). Forth the division of the cut allow a carefully analysis of each type of song and it will be helpful to identify the species in the zone. Finally this division allows for the study of this very interesting intra population vocal variation in these populations of northern andes in Antioquia;  that to my knowledge my recordings in Amalfi and Anori are the first of the species at least in xenocanto, I know that Glenn Seeholzer did some cuts in Amalfi but  are only  present in Macaulay library, so they can't be downloaded sadly for everyone and with limited use at field.

Este individuo, y otros dos más lejos, empezaron a cantar ANTES de las 4.45am por más de una hora hasta que empezó a clariar antes de las 6.00am.

Hay unos finales de frase muy chéveres que no había yo escuchao antes en 6:12, en 11:17 y en 26:44. Luego al 43:22 hay llamados de interacción de estos mismos individuos.

En el 42:33 empiezan a cantar los Bichofués (Pitangus sulphuratus) en el fondo, y luego en el 45:00 empiezan los llamados de interacción que escucho casi que exclusivamente al amanecer (en Medellín pues).

En 6:30 y en 8:00 hay llamados de murciélagos, y luego en 19:14 el ruido de sus alas pasando muy cerca del micrófono... vi unos 6 individuos al mismo tiempo.

En el 28:27 está el guequito introducido Lepidodactylus lugubris

~~~~~~~

This individual bird and at least 2 others, started dawn-singing BEFORE 4.45 AM and it lasted MORE than one full hour until it got lighter just before 6.00 AM

There is a very neat ending of some phrases I had never heard before ie. at 6:12, at 11:17, and also at 26:44. Then, at 43:22 you start hearing interaction calls from these very same individuals.

At 42:33 you can hear the first Great Kiskadees calling in the background, and by 45:00 the cool bizarre interaction calls (almost always heard only at dawn -by me!) that these kiskadees make.

Heavy bat calling at 6:30 and at 8:00, plus bats' wings VERY close to the mic at 19:14 - saw up to 6 individuals.

At 28:27 you can hear the calls of the introduced Lepidodactylus lugubris Gecko.

Around 3 individuals performing their singing from 3 palms (Arecacea) on the roadside. Close to a restaurant for truckers (it explains the sound of trucks).

It is important to stand out the fact that the singing was performed in a special position while perched: raised and folded wings, each wing taking a form  like this: ⋏, just a little above the head of the bird. Before each note the bird seemed to be slightly inflated and puffy (like it was taking some air) and then after the note seemed to be getting back to the original "not-puffy" state. And repeated this all over again (although this was so fast, cause there is a really short interval between notes).

We observed a flock of 6 individuals composed by two juveniles and four adults (probably males) on forest interior of andean montage forest near a stream, foraging mainly on upperstory and canopy , looking for fruits and small arthropods. They did several short stops between trees especially looking for insects into the bark. I consider that the calls can correspond to contact calls and in some cases alarm calls, but looking to Andres Cuervo  recordings in Amalfi and Anori , their social function could be wider at least based in his observations. Recording distance was 10 meters in many cases but change because the individuals changed constantly  of position in the forest. However they always remained close to the stream at least during the afternoon (morning they expended more time in the forest edge and in fact near some gardens adjacent to the stream in the borders of la Estrella.

rmk:
Two birds of approximately equal size and morphology can be listened in this recording, they were next to each other on a wire  above the fence surrounding a urbanization complex. The fence is surrounded on the inside by bushes and on the outside an open area constituted by grass, the type of habitat where birds like Yellow-bellied Seedeater (*Sporophila nigricollis*), Yellow-faced Grassquit (*Tiaris olivaceus*), Blue-black Grassquit (*Volatinia jacarina*) and sometimes Saffron Finch (*Sicalis flaveola*) can be seen. 


**Behavior**

One of them was in the same position while singing and is the one that corresponds to the group of rapid "tsip"notes (between 12 and 28 in this recording, variable) with pauses of  1-10 seconds (that one is clearly a Yellow-faced Grassquit). 
The other one, slightly smaller than the first one corresponds to the two alternating  notes along the recording. While singing this individual (slighly fluffed) was flapping his wings and moving his head from side to side, changing the direction of his body inward and outward the complex's fence once a while (intervals of aprox. 8 sec) without stopping the flapping and the singing. This might be a still immature Yellow-faced Grassquit cause they seemed to be pretty similar and when they left the fence they left flying together in the same direction. On the other hand,  I haven't heard this songtype for this specie. 

Any opinions?

The mystery vocalization is an 8-element song repeated three times on an even pitch. Superficially, it sounds similar to Scrub Greenlet, which was common, but the elements are shaped differently in the sonogram. In the field, I suspected this was Vireolanius eximius (I was without access to other east-slope recordings of this species).  

Whatever it is, it was *common* at this site between 900 masl (the lowest elevation accessed) and 1100 masl.  

At times, it gave long and highly regular series (as heard here extended for several minutes), which raises my suspicion that it could be non-avian.

I felt that it was in the canopy, but the extreme topography of the site made it difficult to confidently assess what strata sounds came from if they were even moderately distant.

The mystery is the dominant sound on the cut, and I suspect it is Thripadectes (flammulatus or holostictus), but it is atypical for either species.  At 0:09, a bird calls that I've identified as Mecocerculus minor (see XC258725 ); let me know if I've got this wrong.
